content.overview: BNS s. 145 — Habitual dealing in slaves.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Habitual dealing in slaves. BNS restatement of IPC 371. Elements are substantially the same; cite the BNS number for offences on or after 1 July 2024. BNS restatement of IPC 371. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 145 is the rule on “Habitual dealing in slaves”. The section provides that whoever habitually imports, exports, removes, buys, sells, traffics or deals in slaves, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term not exceeding ten years, and shall also be liable to fine. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 145 exists so that “Habitual dealing in slaves” has a closed legal test in Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: Homicide, organised crime, terrorism, hurt, acid, restraint, assault, kidnapping and trafficking.

The provision in detail
145. Whoever habitually imports, exports, removes, buys, sells, traffics or deals in slaves, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term not exceeding ten years, and shall also be liable to fine

Essential ingredients
1. Whoever habitually imports, exports, removes, buys, sells, traffics or deals in slaves, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term not exceeding ten years, and shall also be liable to fine

hypotheticals.analysis:
Step 1 — Identify the provision. The correct current-law cite is BNS s. 145 (Habitual dealing in slaves), Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body.
Step 2 — State the legal test in your own words, then list the ingredients:
   (1) Whoever habitually imports, exports, removes, buys, sells, traffics or deals in slaves, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term not exceeding ten years, and shall also be liable to fine
Step 3 — Check limitations, provisos and the rest of the Chapter so you do not apply s. 145 in a vacuum.
Step 4 — Map each fact to an ingredient. Write “this fact proves ingredient (a)” or “this fact is missing, so the section is not made out”.
Step 5 — Conclude. If every essential ingredient is proved and no exception covers the case, BNS s. 145 applies. If any essential ingredient fails, say so and stop. Do not invent a different section to save the answer.

learningObjectives: Master the severe prohibition against slave dealing under BNS s. 145.
Analyze the enumerated commercial acts: importing, exporting, removing, buying, selling, trafficking, or dealing in slaves.
Understand the 'habitual' requirement and evidentiary proof of continuing dealing.
Examine the punishment structure: imprisonment for life or up to ten years, and fine.
Appreciate the consolidation of old IPC s. 371.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 145 penalizes whoever habitually imports, exports, removes, buys, sells, traffics or deals in slaves, with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Absolute abolition of chattel slavery and commercial human bondage, imposing severe life sentences on syndicates and habitual operators dealing in human beings as property.
statutoryFramework: Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body, BNS s. 145 (corresponding to IPC s. 371).
Actus reus: Importing, exporting, removing, buying, selling, trafficking, or dealing in slaves.
Mens rea / Status: Habitually engaging in such transactions.
Punishment: Imprisonment for life, or imprisonment of either description up to ten years, and fine.
Constitutional nexus: Directly enforces the fundamental prohibition against traffic in human beings under Article 23 of the Constitution.
essentialIngredients: The accused engaged in importing, exporting, removing, buying, selling, trafficking, or dealing in human beings as slaves.
The transactions treated persons as chattel property with total deprivation of personal liberty.
The accused engaged in these transactions HABITUALLY (as a repetitive course of conduct or business).
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 145 carries forward Section 371 of the IPC, reflecting India's absolute constitutional and penal repudiation of slavery. The provision targets commercial human chattel brokers. 'Slavery' denotes a condition where one human being exercises absolute ownership, control, and property dominion over another, stripping them of legal rights, freedom of movement, and personal autonomy. Section 145 specifically requires proof of 'habitual' dealing—meaning an ongoing trade, repeated transactions, or a systematic business of buying, selling, or exporting slaves. Because of the grave assault on human dignity, the section provides severe punishment: imprisonment for life, or up to ten years imprisonment, along with fine.
examples: Teaching example (International slave ring): An accused operates an international syndicate that systematically purchases impoverished captives from abroad and sells them into lifelong domestic and agricultural chattel bondage to wealthy patrons. The accused is liable under s. 145 (life imprisonment tier).

Teaching example (Isolated transaction): An accused sells an individual in a single, isolated incident. While the accused is guilty of trafficking under Section 143, Section 145 requires proof of habitual dealing as a pattern.
distinctions: Section 145 vs Section 143: Section 143 covers individual acts of trafficking for exploitation; Section 145 specifically penalizes HABITUAL commercial dealing in slaves.
Section 145 vs Section 146: Section 145 penalizes chattel slavery and dealing (up to life imprisonment); Section 146 penalizes unlawful compulsory labour (up to 1 year).
problemApplication: Issue: Whether a broker who ran a clandestine agency that repeatedly bought and sold captive domestic workers as bonded chattel over five years is punishable under s. 145.
Rule: Habitually buying, selling, or dealing in human beings as slaves constitutes an offence under BNS s. 145.
Application: A continuous commercial course of conduct treating workers as property was proven.
Conclusion: The broker is guilty under BNS s. 145 and faces imprisonment for life.

keyTakeaways: Penalizes habitual dealing, buying, selling, importing, or exporting of slaves.
Direct statutory enforcement of Article 23 of the Constitution.
Requires proof of a habitual commercial course of conduct.
Punishable with imprisonment for life or up to ten years, and fine.
